# ABOUTME: herdr popup helpers: fzf project picker and agent-in-a-new-worktree launcher
# ABOUTME: Packaged by modules/home-manager/herdr.nix; run from [[keys.command]] popups
#
#   herdr-launch project   pick a directory (zoxide frecency first, then git
#                          repos under HERDR_PROJECT_ROOTS) and focus or open
#                          a workspace on it
#   herdr-launch agent KIND...
#                          pick an agent kind, create a git worktree off the
#                          active repo, and start the agent in it

herdr=${HERDR_BIN_PATH:-herdr}
project_roots=${HERDR_PROJECT_ROOTS:-$HOME/src}
worktrees_dir=${HERDR_WORKTREES_DIR:-$HOME/.herdr/worktrees}

# Popups close when the command exits, so hold errors on screen.
fail() {
  printf '\n%s\n' "$*" >&2
  read -rsn1 -p 'press any key' </dev/tty || true
  exit 1
}

# Run a herdr API command, print its JSON, and fail on an error response.
call() {
  local out
  out=$("$herdr" "$@" 2>&1) || true
  if ! jq -e 'has("result")' >/dev/null 2>&1 <<<"$out"; then
    fail "herdr $1 $2: $(jq -r '.error.message // empty' 2>/dev/null <<<"$out" || printf '%s' "$out")"
  fi
  printf '%s\n' "$out"
}

expand_tilde() {
  printf '%s\n' "${1/#\~/$HOME}"
}

project_candidates() {
  zoxide query --list 2>/dev/null || true
  local root roots
  IFS=: read -ra roots <<<"$project_roots"
  for root in "${roots[@]}"; do
    root=$(expand_tilde "$root")
    [ -d "$root" ] || continue
    fd --hidden --type d --max-depth 4 --prune --format '{//}' '^\.git$' "$root" 2>/dev/null | sort
  done
}

cmd_project() {
  local wt pick dir ws
  wt=$(expand_tilde "$worktrees_dir")
  # Keep zoxide's order (recency) and drop duplicates and agent worktrees.
  # fzf's path scheme ranks basename matches first; ties keep input order.
  pick=$(project_candidates |
    awk -v wt="$wt/" -v home="$HOME" '
      index($0, wt) == 1 || seen[$0]++ { next }
      { d = $0; if (index(d, home "/") == 1) d = "~" substr(d, length(home) + 1); print $0 "\t" d }' |
    fzf --delimiter='\t' --with-nth=2 --scheme=path --tiebreak=pathname,index \
      --prompt='project> ' --preview='ls -A --color=always {1}' --preview-window=right,40%) || exit 0
  dir=$(realpath "${pick%%$'\t'*}")
  zoxide add "$dir" 2>/dev/null || true

  # A primary checkout that is already open gets focused instead of duplicated.
  ws=$("$herdr" worktree list --cwd "$dir" 2>/dev/null |
    jq -r --arg d "$dir" '.result.worktrees[]? | select(.path == $d) | .open_workspace_id // empty' 2>/dev/null || true)
  if [ -n "$ws" ]; then
    call workspace focus "$ws" >/dev/null
  else
    call workspace create --cwd "$dir" --focus >/dev/null
  fi
}

cmd_agent() {
  [ $# -gt 0 ] || fail "usage: herdr-launch agent KIND..."
  local cwd common root kind default branch name out pane
  cwd=${HERDR_ACTIVE_PANE_CWD:-$PWD}

  # herdr only creates worktrees from the primary checkout, so resolve it
  # even when the active pane sits in a linked worktree.
  common=$(git -C "$cwd" rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-common-dir 2>/dev/null) ||
    fail "not inside a git repository: $cwd"
  [ "$(basename "$common")" = .git ] || fail "unsupported repository layout: $common"
  root=$(dirname "$common")

  kind=$(printf '%s\n' "$@" | fzf --prompt="agent in $(basename "$root")> " --no-sort) || exit 0
  default="$kind/$(date +%m%d-%H%M)"
  read -rei "$default" -p 'branch: ' branch || exit 0
  branch=${branch:-$default}

  # Agent names must match [a-z][a-z0-9_-]{0,31}.
  name=$(printf '%s' "$branch" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' | tr -c 'a-z0-9_-' '-')
  case $name in [a-z]*) ;; *) name="a$name" ;; esac
  name=${name:0:32}

  out=$(call worktree create --cwd "$root" --branch "$branch" --label "$branch" --focus)
  pane=$(jq -r '.result.root_pane.pane_id' <<<"$out")
  call agent start "$name" --kind "$kind" --pane "$pane" >/dev/null
}

case ${1:-} in
  project) shift; cmd_project "$@" ;;
  agent) shift; cmd_agent "$@" ;;
  *) fail "usage: herdr-launch {project|agent KIND...}" ;;
esac

## What we learned

### Model differences from tmux

- Hierarchy is workspace → tab → pane. A workspace is the per-repo or per-task
  unit. A "session" is a separate server with its own panes and state
  (`herdr session attach <name>`), not a tmux session equivalent.
- Any pane can be a plain shell. Agents (claude, codex, kiro) are recognized
  foreground processes with states `idle`/`working`/`blocked`/`done`.
  `prefix+g` opens the picker (`b` filters blocked); `prefix+o` jumps to the
  notification. This replaces `tmux-jump-bell`.
- Resume after server restart needs an agent integration. Claude and codex have
  them; kiro does not (state-only). `herdr.nix` installs only the binary, not
  the integrations. Low priority, since session restore isn't wanted.
- Scriptable: `herdr agent start|prompt|wait`, `herdr pane run|read|wait-output`,
  plus a socket API.

### Copy mode (documented)

| Action | tmux (current) | herdr |
|---|---|---|
| Enter | `prefix+[` | `prefix+[` (`keys.copy_mode`) |
| Select | `v`, `C-v` rectangle | `v` or `Space`; `V` may select lines; no rectangle found |
| Copy | `y` (tmux-yank → `xclip -selection clipboard -i`) | `y` or `Enter` |
| Search | `/` `?` | `/` `?`, `n` `N` (smart-case) |
| Exit | `q` / `Esc` | `q` / `Esc` |
| Scrollback in editor | none | `prefix+e` (`keys.edit_scrollback`) |

- Copy mode does not pause the pane. Output stays live, and selections track
  live text rather than a snapshot. Resize or alt-screen switch clears them.
- `ui.copy_on_select` defaults to true: mouse drag or double-click copies on release.
- `ui.mouse_capture` defaults to true, so WezTerm's own selection probably needs
  a modifier such as shift.
- Relevant config keys: `ui.copy_on_select`, `ui.mouse_capture`,
  `ui.mouse_scroll_lines`, `ui.toast.clipboard.enabled`,
  `ui.right_click_passthrough_modifier`, `advanced.scrollback_limit_bytes`,
  `keys.clear_pane`, `keys.remote_image_paste` (default `ctrl+v`).

### Not documented (the open questions)

- How herdr writes to the system clipboard: OSC 52 to the outer terminal, or a
  native helper?
- Whether it forwards OSC 52 from inside panes (Claude Code `/copy`). tmux needs
  `allow-passthrough on` for this; I found no herdr equivalent.
- Whether there is an internal paste buffer (tmux `prefix+]`), or whether paste
  is just WezTerm's.
- Whether it has a `prefix+y`-style "copy buffer to clipboard" outside copy mode.

### Gaps versus the tmux setup

- No `tmux-thumbs` equivalent (hint-based copy of paths, hashes, IPs).
- No `prefix+y`.
- No rectangle selection found.
- Current herdr config remaps: prefix `ctrl+j`, detach `prefix+d`, resize on
  `prefix+shift+hjkl`, swap on `prefix+alt+hjkl`. herdr's docs and `prefix+?`
  show the defaults, so they will disagree with this config.

### WSL clipboard context (from `project_wsl_terminal_stack` memory)

- xclip via the X11 WSLg bridge round-trips unicode correctly. `clip.exe` and
  the Wayland bridge (`wl-copy`) corrupt non-ASCII.
- tmux works today because of `allow-passthrough on` (OSC 52 → WezTerm →
  Windows) plus `@override_copy_command` = xclip.
- kiro-cli uses arboard/Wayland, so it is aliased with `WAYLAND_DISPLAY=`.

I'd move `prefix+shift+tab` (your old tmux `BTab`) onto a small script that jumps to the agent that most recently started needing attention. `prefix+B` would stay the picker. That keeps the split you had in tmux, where `B` and `BTab` both ran `tmux-jump-bell`:

| Key | Does |
|---|---|
| `prefix+B` | goto picker; press `b` to filter blocked agents (unchanged) |
| `prefix+shift+tab` | jump straight to the latest agent needing attention (new) |
| `prefix+o` | herdr's built-in notification target (unchanged) |

This keeps your muscle memory and doesn't use up a new key. It also fixes something that's probably broken now. `shift+tab` is currently bound to `open_notification_target`, which according to herdr's docs focuses "the currently visible notification target". Your config sends notifications to WezTerm (`ui.toast.delivery = "terminal"`) instead of showing them inside herdr. So there's likely never a visible target, and that key does nothing most of the time. I haven't tested this. Press `prefix+o` after an agent finishes to check.

**Why it needs a script:** herdr 0.9.3 has no built-in "most recent attention" action. Its closest options don't do it:
- `next_agent` / `previous_agent` step through the sidebar in order.
- `ui.agent_panel_sort = "priority"` changes that order, but it doesn't track recency.

The data it needs is there, though. `herdr agent list` gives each agent an `agent_status` and a `state_change_seq` counter. The script would:
1. Take the agents that aren't focused and whose status is `blocked` or `done`.
2. Prefer `blocked`, since those are waiting on you. Then pick the one with the highest `state_change_seq`, i.e. the most recent.
3. Run `herdr agent focus` on it, or show "nothing needs attention", like `tmux-jump-bell`'s "No bell windows".

That's about ten lines added to `herdr-launch.sh` as a new subcommand, plus the binding change and a README table update.

Not built in. herdr 0.9.3 has no setting like tmux's `automatic-rename`. A new tab is just labeled with its number until you rename it with `prefix+shift+t`. I checked the config reference and herdr's issue tracker and found neither an option nor a feature request for it.

It can be added from zsh, though. Every pane already sets `HERDR_PANE_ID` and `HERDR_TAB_ID`, and `herdr tab rename <TAB_ID> <LABEL>` works from inside a pane. A herdr CLI call takes about 8ms here, and the hooks would run it in the background so the prompt never waits. The plan:

- **preexec hook:** before a command runs, rename the tab to the command name (`nvim`, `ssh`, `claude`, …). It would strip Nix's `.foo-wrapped` names the same way your tmux `automatic-rename-format` does.
- **precmd hook:** when the prompt comes back, set the tab back to `zsh`, as tmux shows the shell when nothing is running. I could use the directory name instead if you'd find that more useful.
- **Leave manual names alone:** before each rename, check the current label. If it's neither the herdr default (a number) nor the last name the hook set, you named the tab yourself, so leave it. Without this check, the next command would overwrite your names.
- **Only outside herdr-free shells:** do nothing unless `HERDR_ENV` is set, so shells outside herdr behave as before.

It would go in `modules/home-manager/zsh.nix`, or behind a small `webframp.herdr.autoRenameTabs` option if you'd rather keep it with the herdr config.

**Limits compared with tmux:**
- tmux names a window after its active pane. These hooks fire in whichever pane ran the last command, so in a tab with split panes, a command in a background pane renames the tab too.
- Moving between panes doesn't change the name until you run something.
- Only zsh panes get renamed. A pane started directly as an agent, without a shell, keeps its label. An agent you start by typing `claude` at the prompt does get renamed, since the hook sees that command.

I can implement it if you want. One question first: when the prompt is idle, should the tab say `zsh`, as tmux does, or show the directory name?

Tabs now take the name of the command running in their zsh pane, and show `zsh` at an idle prompt. It's all in the herdr module; `zsh.nix` is untouched. `make nixos-build` passes, but you still need to apply it.

**Tested in a throwaway herdr tab** with the hooks loaded:

| Step | Tab label |
|---|---|
| New tab after the first prompt | `zsh` (instead of a number) |
| `true` (finishes instantly) | `zsh` |
| While `sleep 3` runs | `sleep` |
| After `sleep 3` | `zsh` |
| While `FOO=1 command less /etc/hostname` runs | `less` (env assignment and `command` skipped) |
| After quitting `less` | `zsh` |
| Renamed by hand to `mywork`, then ran a command | stayed `mywork` |

**Changes:**
- `home/sme/shared/includes/herdr-tab-name.zsh` (new): the zsh hooks. They do nothing outside herdr. I marked the file with `git add -N` so the flake build can see it; nothing else is staged by me.
- `herdr-launch.sh`: a new `tab-name` subcommand, which the hooks run in the background so the prompt never waits.
- `herdr.nix`:
  - a `webframp.herdr.autoRenameTabs` option, on by default
  - adds the hook file to `programs.zsh.initContent`
  - adds `flock` to the launcher's dependencies
- `README.org`: a line under the Herdr table about the auto-naming.

**A race I found and fixed:** a fast command like `true` could finish before its rename landed, and the late rename then left the tab named `true` at an idle prompt. Each rename now carries a timestamp, and a per-pane lock drops any rename that a newer one has already replaced. The `true` row above is the test of this.

**Limits:**
- The name comes from the command as typed: the first word of a pipeline (`cat x | less` shows `cat`), and an alias's own name.
- In a tab with split panes, whichever pane ran the last command names the tab.
- Tabs you've already named keep their names; any tab still showing a plain number is renamed by the next command.

To apply it, run `make nixos-switch`, then `herdr server reload-config` for the keybinding changes. The tab naming only starts in shells opened after the switch.

## WSL Terminal Stack (galvatron-wsl)

**Architecture:** WezTerm (Windows, winget) → WSL:NixOS → tmux → zsh → tools (claude, kiro-cli, opencode)

### Clipboard Pipeline
- **KEY FINDING (2026-07):** `xclip` (X11) via the WSLg bridge round-trips unicode **both ways** to the Windows clipboard correctly — verified by writing with xclip and reading with `win32yank.exe -o`, and vice-versa. So win32yank.exe is NOT required for correct UTF-8; it's redundant with xclip. What DOES corrupt non-ASCII: `clip.exe`, and the **Wayland** bridge (`wl-copy`). The X11 bridge does not. (Caveat: `powershell.exe Get-Clipboard` writes stdout in the console codepage — an unreliable readback that looks like corruption but isn't. Use `win32yank.exe -o` to verify what's actually on the Windows clipboard.)
- **Decision (2026-07):** dropped Windows-interop clipboard deps in favor of xclip. `webframp.tmux.copyCommand = "xclip -selection clipboard -i"`; `pbcopy`/`pbpaste` aliases → xclip; `qp`/`qpo` (pass) → `WAYLAND_DISPLAY= pass -c` (see below).
- **OSC 52** (Claude Code `/copy`) → tmux `allow-passthrough on` → WezTerm → Windows clipboard (UTF-8 correct)
- **`pass -c` / `qp`:** pass's `clip()` prefers `WAYLAND_DISPLAY` (→ wl-copy, not installed) over `DISPLAY` (→ xclip). WSLg now exports `WAYLAND_DISPLAY=wayland-0`, so plain `qp` broke. Fix: prefix with `WAYLAND_DISPLAY=` to force the xclip branch.
- **kiro-cli** uses arboard/Wayland clipboard → WSLg bridge corrupts non-ASCII. Fix: alias `kiro-cli` with `WAYLAND_DISPLAY=` to force X11 fallback (same mechanism as `qp`).

### Windows interop PATH gotcha
Under NixOS-WSL with `[boot] systemd=true`, the Windows PATH is NOT appended to interactive shells even though `/etc/wsl.conf` has `appendWindowsPath=true` and the `WSLInterop` binfmt is registered. So bare `clip.exe`/`win32yank.exe`/`powershell.exe`/`wsl.exe` do not resolve (nothing under `/mnt/c` is on `$PATH`). The `.exe` files exist on disk and run fine by absolute path. Genuine Windows-only calls (`restart-wslg` → `wsl.exe`, Doom org-download image paste → `powershell.exe`) are pinned to absolute `/mnt/c/...` paths for this reason.

### Notifications
- Tools send BEL (`\a`) on task completion
- WezTerm `bell` event hook fires toast notification via `window:toast_notification`
- `config.audible_bell = "Disabled"` — no sound
- `window:is_focused()` check — only toast when alt-tabbed away
- tmux statusbar highlights bell windows in red (dracula override in tmux.conf)
- `C-j Shift-Tab` / `C-j B` — jump to first window with pending bell (uses `~/.local/bin/tmux-jump-bell` script because tmux `run-shell` expands `#{}` formats before execution)

### Known Constraints
- `\e]777;notify` escape sequences do NOT pass through tmux (tmux strips unknown OSCs, `allow-passthrough` only works for DCS-wrapped sequences)
- WezTerm sees one pane (tmux), so pane title/user vars reflect whichever tmux window last set them, not the window that sent the bell
- Toast notifications require WezTerm installed via winget (not scoop) — Windows requires app registration for toasts
- `audible_bell = "Disabled"` in WezTerm config doesn't fully suppress on older versions; disable via Windows Settings → Notifications → WezTerm → uncheck sound

# WSLg Crash Resilience

## Goal

Stop WSLg compositor crashes from costing a working session. Two tracks: make the
editor workflow survive a weston death (fully in our control), and gather enough
evidence to either pin the WSL version or file a usable upstream bug (not in our
control).

Explicit non-goal: fixing weston itself. It runs inside the WSLg system distro
image, which we do not build or control.

## Current State

Emacs runs as `emacs-pgtk-with-packages-30.2`, a Wayland-native client of WSLg's
weston. When weston dies, the editor dies with it, and WSLg does not come back
without a full `wsl --shutdown`. Frequency has increased noticeably over recent
weeks.

1. **The permanence is a supervisor policy, not a deeper failure.** WSLGd retries

# fast-jev-compaction

Claude Code plugin that replaces the compaction summary with Jev decisions:
every tool call and result is scored in one fast request, stale ones are
dropped or truncated, everything kept stays verbatim. Also usable as an npm
library.

## What and why

Most context compaction asks an LLM to summarize old turns. A summary is
lossy: a file path, exact error, constraint, or command can disappear even when
it matters later. This library never rewrites anything. It only deletes tool
calls and tool results Jev says are no longer needed, and it asks Jev while
showing it the whole conversation. User and assistant text stays verbatim and
in order.

The repository is both an npm package (`src/`) and a Claude Code plugin
(`hooks/`, `.claude-plugin/`) that uses the package to replace Claude Code's
built-in compaction summary with the original messages.

## How it works

1. Every `tool_use` is paired with its `tool_result` by `tool_use_id`. Calls in
   the first message or in the newest `preserveRecentMessages` messages are
   pinned and never touched.
2. The **state** sent to Jev is the whole conversation so far, oldest first,
   with every tool result replaced by a short note (`ok, 4213 chars (omitted)`).
   Tool inputs are included, texts are included, nothing is summarized.
3. The state is fitted into `maxStateTokens` (25k by default) in stages, each
   applied only if the previous one was not enough: tool inputs truncated to
   1000, then 200, then 60 characters; long texts abridged to head + tail,
   oldest non-pinned messages first; old non-pinned messages collapsed to a
   `[… N chars omitted …]` note; old tool calls reduced to one line each
   (`t12 Read file_path=src/a.ts → ok 480ch`); old call-less messages left
   out; runs of old call-only messages folded into one entry. If it still
   does not fit, compaction throws. Tokens are estimated without a tokenizer (a
   word per six letters, half a token per digit, ~one per other symbol),
   calibrated to land a little above the counts Jev reports.
4. For every non-pinned call Jev gets two `noul` questions: should the **call**
   stay (knowing it was made, with its input, still matters), and should the
   **result** stay verbatim (its contents are still needed and re-running the
   tool would not do).
5. Questions are split into as many requests as needed so state plus questions
   stays under `maxRequestTokens` (30k by default, under Jev's 32k request
   limit). The same full state is resent with every request; requests run
   concurrently and their answers are merged.
6. Decisions per call, against `keepThreshold`:
   - `keepResult ≥ threshold` → keep call and result;
   - else `keepCall ≥ threshold` → keep the call, truncate the result to its
     first `truncateHeadChars` characters plus a one-line note;
   - else → remove the call together with its result.
7. The message list is rebuilt: a message that loses all its content is
   removed, untouched messages are returned as the same objects, and no result
   is ever left without its call.

Jev failures, malformed answers, a missing key, or a history that cannot be
fitted throw; the caller (or the Claude Code hook) decides what to fall back to.

## Install and usage

```sh
npm install fast-jev-compaction
export TYPESAFE_API_KEY=...
```

```ts
import { compactMessages, reductionRatio, type Message } from 'fast-jev-compaction';

const transcript: Message[] = [
  { role: 'user', text: 'Fix the failing test. Never edit src/generated.', toolUses: [] },
  {
    role: 'assistant',
    text: '',
    toolUses: [{ tool_use_id: 'toolu_1', tool: 'Read', input: { file_path: 'src/a.ts' } }],
  },
  { role: 'user', text: '', toolUses: [], toolResults: [{ tool_use_id: 'toolu_1', text: '…file…' }] },
  // …
];

const result = await compactMessages(transcript, { preserveRecentMessages: 4 });
console.log(result.messages, result.decisions, result.stats);
if (reductionRatio(result) < 0.25) {
  // not worth it: keep the original transcript, or summarize instead
}
```

`Message` is a subset of Claude Code's `SessionMessage`, so a session transcript
can be passed in as is.

To bring your own transport, implement `JevAsker` (one `ask(state, questions)`
method) and call `compact(messages, asker, options)`; `buildJevRequest` and
`parseJevResponse` give you the HTTP request body and response validation.
The building blocks (`collectToolCalls`, `fitState`, `batchCalls`,
`decideCall`, `applyDecisions`) are exported too.

`apiKey` defaults to `process.env.TYPESAFE_API_KEY`. Never commit the key or
put it in a source file.

## Options

| Option | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `apiKey` | `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` | TypeSafe API key (`compactMessages`/`JevClient`) |
| `model` | `jev-latest` | Jev model name |
| `baseUrl` | `https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone` | System One endpoint |
| `fetch` | native `fetch` | Injectable fetch implementation for tests |
| `goal` | last 3 user prompts | Ongoing task description included in the state |
| `keepThreshold` | `0.5` | Minimum keep probability for a call or result to stay |
| `preserveRecentMessages` | `6` | Newest messages never touched (the first is always kept) |
| `maxStateTokens` | `25000` | Estimated token ceiling for the state |
| `maxRequestTokens` | `30000` | Estimated ceiling for state plus one batch of questions |
| `truncateHeadChars` | `300` | Characters of a dropped tool result retained before its note |

`result.stats` reports message and character counts before and after, the
per-reason decision counts, the state size in estimated tokens, which fitting
stage was needed, and the number of requests.

## Limitations

- Only tool calls and results are candidates; text messages are never removed
  or shortened in the output (they are only abridged in the state Jev sees).
- Token sizes are estimates from character counts, not a tokenizer.
- Calibration is at the request level; a probability is not a proof that a
  result is safe to delete. The assistant can always re-run the tool.
- The full state is repeated with every request, so a history near the state
  ceiling costs one request per handful of questions.

## Claude Code plugin

The repository root is a Claude Code function-hook plugin: `hooks/fast-jev.ts`
is a thin adapter that feeds `session.compact` transcripts through `src/` and
falls back to Claude Code's built-in summary on errors or insufficient
reduction. See [`hooks/README.md`](hooks/README.md) for configuration and the
Claude Code 2.1.274 type reference.

### Install in Claude Code

Function hooks are an early-access Claude Code feature (2.1.274+), so the
opt-in flag must be set wherever Claude Code runs, e.g. in `~/.claude/settings.json`:

```json
{ "env": { "CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS": "1", "TYPESAFE_API_KEY": "<your key>" } }
```

Then add this repository as a plugin marketplace and install the plugin,
either from the shell or as slash commands inside a session:

```sh
claude plugin marketplace add tamaratran/fast-jev-compaction
claude plugin install fast-jev-compaction@fast-jev-compaction
```

The install prompts for the plugin options (API key, thresholds, `truncateHeadChars`,
…); leave them at their defaults to use `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` from the environment.
Restart Claude Code or run `/reload-plugins`. From then on `/compact` (and
auto-compaction) goes through Jev: the toast reads
`fast-jev-compaction: kept N/M messages, no summary (…)` when the pruned history
replaced the built-in summary, or `fallback to built-in summary (…)` when Jev
could not remove enough (short sessions, or when it fails).

To run from a checkout without installing: `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1 claude --plugin-dir .`
from the repository root. No publishing step is required; the marketplace is
just the repo's `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`.

content.text:
Fast-jev-compaction replaces Claude Code's compaction summary with pruning. Instead of having a model rewrite your history into a summary, it asks TypeSafe's Jev model which old tool calls and results are still needed. It then drops the stale ones and keeps everything else word for word. I read all of its code, and it's safe to try, with one real question first: what it sends to TypeSafe.

## How it works

- **Keeps your text exactly.** Your messages and Claude's replies are never removed or rewritten. Only old tool calls and their results are candidates.
- **Decides per tool call.** For each call older than the newest 6 messages, Jev scores two questions: is the call still needed, and is its full output still needed?
  - Output still needed: kept in full.
  - Only the call needed: the output is cut to its first 300 characters plus a note.
  - Neither: the call and its output are removed.
- **Falls back safely.** If the API key is missing, Jev returns an error, or pruning would save less than 25%, it uses Claude Code's normal summary instead.
- **Compacts on its own.** It also starts compaction at 60% context usage. Claude Code's automatic compaction waits much longer, so this changes how often you compact.

The trade-off: a summary can quietly lose an exact path, error message, or constraint. This keeps those intact and drops whole tool outputs, which Claude can get back by running the tool again.

## What leaves your machine

On every compaction, it sends a POST to `https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone` containing:

- **Sent:** every message you and Claude wrote, every tool input (commands, file paths, edit contents cut to 1000 characters), and the text of your last 3 prompts as the "goal".
- **Not sent:** the contents of tool results. Each one is replaced by a note such as `ok, 4213 chars (omitted)`.

That's the real decision. It's a third-party service, and your sessions include work context: AWS, Microsoft 365 through MCP, and internal repos. I haven't checked TypeSafe's data retention or training policy, so read it first, and decide whether work sessions should go there at all.

## Code review

- **Small and clean.** About 1,000 lines of TypeScript with no runtime dependencies. It has exactly one outbound URL, and no filesystem, shell, or process access. The API key goes only in that one request's header.
- **Brand new.** The repo was created on 2026-09-17 and has a single commit, despite 7.6k stars. Installing from its marketplace follows the repo's latest commit, so future changes would arrive without review.
- **Early-access hooks.** It uses a Claude Code feature behind `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1` that needs version 2.1.274 or later. You have 2.1.284. These hooks run inside Claude Code with access to your session.

## Setup

- **API key:** don't follow the README here. It says to put `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` in `~/.claude/settings.json`, but your copy is a symlink to `config/claude/settings.json` in this repo, so the key would be committed. Use one of these instead:
  - the plugin's own `apiKey` prompt at install, which is marked sensitive and isn't written to settings
  - exporting `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` from `pass` in your shell
- **Pin the version:** run it from a checkout at a fixed commit with `--plugin-dir` rather than installing from its marketplace, so updates only arrive when you review them.
- **Try it on personal sessions first,** such as dotfiles or blog work. Compare its compaction notifications (percentage saved, what it kept and dropped) against the normal summary before you decide on work use.
